topic: distributed/cloud systems; energy-aware scheduling; building IoT; LLM serving
status: four fixed-frame uniform-random full texts across four arXiv submission periods; bounded measurement-design hypothesis, not pooled effect
claim: In this sample, resource-efficiency claims are conditional on the service quality the system is allowed to sacrifice and on how success is counted. The 2013 cloud scheduler pauses opted-in VMs for four hours/day and empirically lowers energy/cost while also reducing computation; the 2015 building paper has a long observational building trace but only a short one-user prototype comparison against partly estimated modes; the 2023 GPT-cloud paper proposes schedulers without an executed benchmark; the 2025 SLINFER paper measures requests meeting explicit TTFT/TPOT SLOs under a particular workload/hardware configuration. Therefore headline savings/capacity percentages are not directly comparable and must not be interpreted as a historical efficiency trend.

sources.title: Take a break: cloud scheduling optimized for real-time electricity pricing
locators: §IV-V: 24-hour one-VM comparison; ~5.3% measured energy and ~6.9% calculated price reductions; four fewer CPU hours/17.6% fewer computations
§V-B/Table I: synthetic projection assumes idealized energy-proportional hardware; 17.1% energy, 26.63% price and 83.3% availability
§VI: future work calls for additional workload types

sources.title: An Internet of Things Framework for Smart Energy in Buildings: Designs, Prototype, and Experiments
locators: §II: nearly one year of traces from one LEED-Gold office building
§IV: 24-hour user-scale location/device prototype compared to estimated use modes
§IV and conclusion: effects may differ across buildings and occupant habits; venue year 2015, arXiv deposit 2016

sources.title: Resource Management for GPT-based Model Deployed on Clouds: Challenges, Solutions, and Future Directions
locators: §3-4: proposed architecture and three resource-placement algorithms
§4 algorithms: rely on abstract resource/power-estimation functions
§5: standardized benchmarks and comprehensive metrics remain future work; no comparative experiment in this paper

sources.title: Towards Resource-Efficient Serverless LLM Inference with SLINFER
locators: §IX-A: four 32-core Xeon 6462C CPU nodes, four A100-80GB GPU nodes, sampled Azure traces, and TTFT/TPOT SLOs
§IX-B: 128-model capacity results—47-62% over sllm+c and 86-154% over sllm for SLO-met requests
§III-B and §IX-I: model/workload-specific benefit; long-input, old non-AMX CPU, tight-SLO and large-model limitations

interpretation: A measurement/reporting gap is visible across these examples, not a claim that unlike systems should share one benchmark or that any cited paper is invalid. The common comparison variable is resource consumed per successful task at a declared service-quality boundary; availability, completion, latency, output/task correctness, workload, and hardware need to be explicit before comparing efficiency. The 2023 paper is proposal-level evidence, unlike the empirical studies.
falsifiable_question: When resource use is compared against tuned baselines at preregistered and matched service-quality targets, do the reported efficiency/capacity benefits persist on held-out real workloads and hardware after counting rejected, timed-out, paused, or lower-quality tasks and transition/idle costs?
primary_outcome: Resource or cost per successful task at matched service-quality levels, with a Pareto curve across availability/completion, latency distribution, and task/output correctness; separately report energy, monetary cost, accepted/rejected requests, and workload/hardware coverage.
counterevidence_and_caveats: The 2013 cloud study directly shows that users may accept reduced availability in exchange for price/energy benefits; such an SLA tradeoff can be a valid product rather than a flaw.

The 2015 building study includes a year of real building traces and a functioning prototype, so it is stronger than a purely conceptual proposal; the limitation is causal scope of its short, single-user savings demonstration.

SLINFER evaluates explicit TTFT/TPOT constraints on a real multi-node testbed and multiple sensitivity settings; it is not merely an abstract proposal. Its capacity results remain trace-, baseline-, SLO-, and hardware-dependent.
The 2023 framework is algorithmic proposal evidence without an executed comparison, so it cannot support a measured efficiency claim.
Four papers from one sampled topic cell/time design cannot estimate prevalence, establish a temporal trend, or support global novelty.
suggested_design: For each system, preregister a service envelope (availability/completion, latency distribution, and task/output correctness or quality), then sweep that envelope and report resource/cost per successful task against a tuned baseline. Use held-out real traces, workloads, and hardware; count rejected, timed-out, paused, or quality-degraded tasks; include transitions and idle periods in energy/cost. Keep unlike application domains separate and compare within-domain Pareto curves rather than pooling headline percentages.
